entries.title: Allies & Enemies
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Blaming Canada. An exclusive look at a new report on voters known as “Trump Regretters.” The Pentagon’s money problems. A first look at ads attacking Medicare for All. Kalshi vs. regulators. Reality vs USPS ballot rules. And: A look at opportunity zones, eight years later.





THE LATEST

Drinking the anti-Canadian Club? The White House’s fight with America’s northern neighbor continues, trapping border-state Republicans in a conundrum: Do they join up with Donald Trump’s rhetorical crusade and set sail across Lake America looking for a fight? Or do they try to keep up a relationship with a longtime economic partner that is often crucial to a significant number of their constituents?

“I want to get the train back on the tracks. And I think we can do that,” Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Michigan) told NOTUS’ Manuela Silva this week — not exactly chastising Trump but not exactly praising him, either.

Another tough one for Republicans! Cross Trump and there could be political trouble from MAGA; join in the attacks on Canada and there could be political problems at home. “I’m not a big fan of the current situation because Indiana’s a big trading partner with Canada, so I prefer the issue go away,” Republican Rep. Mark Messmer said.

There were some Republicans eager to sign on to Trump’s approach to Canada: “I would hope NOTUS is going to say, ‘Thank you, President Trump, for finally leveling the playing field, taking care of our farmers,’” said Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan, the House Republican Conference chair.

“I stay out of all the back-and-forth,” Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-New York) said. She had plenty of complaints about Canadian trade practices — “so much dumping of powdered milks” — but she stressed that her strong relationships with Canadian lawmakers continue, and urged people not to get too anxious.

“Somehow, I think this shall pass,” she said. Barrett, McClain and Tenney, by the way, were at the Rose Garden dinner with Trump last night.

Could that anxiety create more “Trump Regretters” in the swing seats? Navigator Research, the Democratic-leaning messaging firm, is out with a big new report on this set of potential 2026 voters, NOTUS’ Alex Roarty reports. Using survey and focus-group findings, the firm digs in on Trump 2024 supporters who have hung up their red hats. “One-in-five 2024 Trump voters now regret their vote, especially younger Americans, Black and Latino Americans, independents or non-MAGA Republicans, and moms,” the report finds. “Rising costs and expensive wars among top reasons why Trump voters now regret their vote.”

More on NOTUS: ‘Darn Unusual’ DOJ Filing Has the Trump Administration on Different Path | Strategists Say Battleground Democrats Won’t Be Able to Easily Shake ‘Woke 1.0’ | Federal Judge Blocks Trump’s Latest Effort to Restrict Birthright Citizenship





From the Pentagon


Cash crunch: The stopgap funding bill the House passed to keep the government open through the midterms does not provide the tens of billions of dollars the Pentagon says it needs to cover Iran operations, replenish munitions and sustain forces whose deployments have been extended. NOTUS’ Joe Gould and Avani Kalra report on how some observers see the budget moving forward: There’s a narrow window (like three weeks) for another reconciliation bill to be passed by the Republicans in both chambers. Barring that, the DOD is going to have to figure out how to stretch pennies until after the election.

From the campaign trail


First on NOTUS: Republicans run against “Medicare for All.” A new six-figure ad buy is launching today in D.C. from Seniors Matter for America, a group connected to Trump 1.0 press secretary Sean Spicer. The ads take aim at Democratic candidates over the signature health care proposal backed by progressives, which the group calls “pushing everyone into one government system run by federal bureaucrats.” What you’ll be hearing: “Seniors will show up in November, and the choice couldn’t be more clear: The Republicans fighting for their benefits or the Democrats destroying them?”

More: FEC to Klobuchar: Explain Your $42,000 ‘Asset Transfer’ Between Campaigns | Elon Musk’s Super PAC Dumped $800K Into Battleground Races in August

From K Street


More like K-alshi Street: The prediction market company now has over two-dozen federal lobbyists working on its behalf, including some heavy hitters from across the political spectrum — former Democratic Sen. Blanche Lincoln is one, veteran Republican cloakroom staffer Tony Hanagan is another. As NOTUS’ Mark Alfred reports, this army of influence is up against a growing tide of pro-regulation electeds — and so far, the potential regulations are languishing.

More: New Jersey Takes Its Fight Against Kalshi to the Supreme Court

From the Hill


First on NOTUS: Taking on detention centers. Rep. Veronica Escobar (D-Texas) is introducing legislation that would put new requirements on DHS before it can establish new detention facilities, just weeks after the department scrapped a plan to convert a warehouse in her district to hold immigrants. Some of the requirements the legislation would impose: consulting with local officials, holding public meetings and analyzing potential resource strain.

More: Russia Sanctions Bill Remains Stalled Despite Pressure From Zelenskyy’s Top Envoy

From the White House


Special guest: The White House announced Vice President JD Vance will brief reporters today, filling the void as temporary press secretary for the day. It will be the first briefing since July 23.

Ring ring: Trump debuted a new phone on the Resolute Desk, trimmed in gold, of course. The White House didn’t respond to questions about where it came from or who designed the new device. And neither did Cisco, whose name adorns the top. Don’t confuse the new desk phone with the other gold Trump Phone, which didn’t work out so well.

More: Trump Says White House Helipad Is Complete | Trump Is Planning a Midterm Travel Blitz to Alaska and Other Battlegrounds





THE BIG ONE

One part of the new USPS mail-ballot rule is so time consuming that it’s all but impossible, election officials and experts say. NOTUS’ Eric Katz and Adora Brown report on the various timelines local officials have said it would take to send outgoing mail ballots as required under the new rules — 66,000 hours, or more than seven years, of staff time in Colorado; between 25,000 and 50,000 hours in Oregon.

“It would take about 4.9 years of continuous scanning to verify the whole mailing,” said Tammy Patrick, a former federal compliance officer for elections in Maricopa County, Arizona.

Inside the USPS, some are not feeling much more confident. While the USPS requirements mark a completely new procedure for the agency, postmasters who run the facilities that will receive ballots have yet to be given any guidance for carrying them out, a senior Postal Service source told NOTUS.

A federal court has temporarily blocked the new rules and a number of states continue to push back against them.





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

The hundreds of millions of books the late, great Dolly Parton gave to kids wasn’t just an impressive act of charity, writes NOTUS’ Kainaz Amaria. It created a common reading list in a society that desperately needs one.

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: Plane Carrying DHS Secretary Makes Emergency Landing at DCA, by Kendall Staton

Talk to Tom: Where to Go for a Celebratory Dinner, by Tom Sietsema





NEW ON NOTUS

Missed opportunity? “This is the first I’ve heard about this program,” a rural county treasurer in Illinois told NOTUS’ Jade Lozada about opportunity zones. It’s been eight years since the federal government began a tax-incentive program, dubbed “opportunity zones,” aimed at attracting economic development in low-income areas across the country. As the Treasury Department fields nominations for a second round of the program, Jade looks at where it’s worked (hint: bigger cities) and it hasn’t (rural areas).

entries.title: Are ‘Opportunity Zones’ Creating Opportunity? Rural America Is Waiting.
entries.summary: Local officials tell NOTUS they haven’t seen investment dollars pour in. But they’re welcoming the coming changes to the tax program.
entries.content:
Montgomery County, Illinois, is roughly 700 square miles of sparsely populated land almost perfectly situated in between Springfield and St. Louis. It’s home to a Route 66 Welcome Center and, if a federal tax-incentive program is successful, is supposed to be a hotspot for new economic development.

But when Mike Plunkett, a county coordinator whose job it is to field those millions of dollars in investment, looks around, he wonders why a developer would come there.

“What do we have to offer that a million other Midwestern communities don’t have? We have very little competitive advantage,” Plunkett said.

In the eight years since the federal government implemented “opportunity zones,” a tax-incentive program that aims to spur economic development in selected low-income census tracts in the U.S., many counties have been experiencing what Montgomery has.

As the Treasury Department fields nominations from governors’ offices for the second round of opportunity zone investments this summer — tracts that will be eligible for tax-incentivized investments starting in January 2027 — communities are wondering whether they will actually experience the benefits of the program this time.

Plunkett said he has received only one inquiry about the program: from a construction gear manufacturer that set up shop in Montgomery County.

“There have been no other inquiries about the opportunity zone,” Plunkett added.

Multiple local officials from around the country reached by NOTUS said they weren’t aware their county was in an opportunity zone. “This is the first I’ve heard about this program,” said a rural county treasurer in Illinois, who requested anonymity for fear of retaliation. “There isn’t any attraction to come here.”

The average rural zone attracted just $7.3 million in investment from 2018 to 2024, compared to $23.3 million for the average nonrural opportunity zone, according to a June paper by the Treasury’s Office of Tax Analysis. In total, 16% of opportunity zone property was in rural areas, even though it makes up 38% of the U.S.’s 8,764 opportunity zones. In all, $112 billion has been invested using opportunity zone tax incentives.

There’s no comprehensive federal tracking of the impact of opportunity zones, but outside research has shown the program yielding mixed results. Opportunity zones have spurred the construction of 416,000 new homes, according to one paper from the Economic Innovation Group, a think tank that leads the pack in measuring the program’s impact. They have created new jobs, most of which go to residents from more affluent areas outside of the opportunity zone, reports another from the National Bureau of Economic Research. They have no significant effect on commercial investment and business activity, says a third by economists Naomi Feldman and Kevin Corinth, who is a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

Local economic development officials largely said they felt the incentives were not properly promoted.

Corey Proctor, the planning director for Forrest County, Mississippi, said his county needs new housing and has vast swathes of land he believes could attract industry, but local developers lack the requisite information to leverage the tax incentive.

Those developers could benefit from workshops that provide a rundown on how to invest in an opportunity zone, whether delivered by his office or the state or federal government, Proctor said.

“It’d be good to have everyone on the same page,” he said.

Last year’s budget reconciliation law does seek to remedy the rural investment disparity.

Opportunity zones allow taxpayers to invest capital gains income from stocks or property into funds that back development projects in low-income tracts. In return, investors can defer and reduce their tax payments on their gains. After 10 years invested in the fund, gains on the opportunity zone investment itself are completely tax free.

Starting next year, investors in newly created rural opportunity zone funds will receive a 30% reduction in their capital gains tax bill after five years invested in a rural opportunity zone, compared to 10% for nonrural zones.

Rural counties can’t offer the scores of people to fill shiny new apartment complexes and office buildings, or the transit infrastructure to support construction that their urban competitors for opportunity zone dollars can. They also typically lack the robust economic development teams with arsenals of resources for investors to utilize that many cities leverage.

That puts rural counties in a tough spot. With limited county staff and few established local investors, rural county leaders said attracting opportunity zone investment will require an unprecedented effort by local economic planners to read up on opportunity zones and pitch their own to developers — work that they currently don’t do or don’t know about.

Local officials told NOTUS that having extensive data on the impact of opportunity zone investments could help draw in new investors.

Currently, no one — neither the developers, nor the opportunity zone municipalities or the Treasury Department — bears the explicit responsibility to measure the program’s impact before changes in last year’s budget reconciliation law. Investors currently need only submit basic data on the value and the location of their property holdings on annual tax forms.

Under the latest budget law, however, investors must report the numbers of residential units held and full-time workers employed in the fund’s businesses, as well as the basic data on their investments. Congress allocated $15 million for the Treasury to produce annual reports enumerating opportunity zones’ housing and job creation, as well as less-frequent reports detailing the impact of investment on metrics such as poverty and unemployment rates and median family income.

“That would be on my wishlist for opportunity zone 2.0 is to really strengthen the reporting mechanisms so that communities truly can major those ROIs,” said Kersten Swinyard, the economic development director for Salt Lake County, Utah. “We’d love to be able to highlight these numbers. We just don’t have them.”

Localities that have successfully drawn investment do not have a clear picture of the program’s impact — or take pains to estimate it. Though she lacked impact data, Swinyard said opportunity zones were an undeniable success in Salt Lake County, where the tax incentive helped attract large logistics and industrial projects, as well as housing and commercial development.

“Opportunity zones can be either a useful way to channel investment to places that really need it or a tax shelter with high abuse potential, and the determining factor as to which side wins out is precisely the type of tracking and evaluation that is required, and that we've never seen quite enough of,” said Jared Bernstein, the chief economic adviser to then-President Joe Biden who co-authored the original 2015 paper proposing opportunity zones with Kevin Hassett, the current National Economic Council director.

The program’s impact is hard to grasp even on the ground and even in urban areas with more resources.

In Washington, D.C., which has raked in $1.2 billion in opportunity zone investment, the mayor’s office and developers are trying their own hands at data-gathering to paint a picture of the program that will keep investors coming back.

The mayor’s office cobbles together assessments through its building permitting process, conversations with developers about how much capital they’ve deployed and job estimates configured by the city’s tax revenue and licensing offices, said Nina Albert, the deputy mayor for economic planning and development.

RedBrick LMD, one of the largest private landowners in D.C., has hired a third-party firm to evaluate their opportunity zone investments for the purpose of pitching to impact investors.

Opportunity zone projects like those of RedBrick have transformed pockets of the city, particularly in Anacostia, Congress Heights and Barry Farm.

Aside a bend in the Anacostia River, facing the white arches of the Frederick Douglass Memorial Bridge stretching to Navy Yard, RedBrick erected the Bridge District towers — a swanky mixed-income and mixed-use development with a plant wall in the lobby and a pool on the rooftop. A brewery and coffee shop sit on the ground floor.

The Bridge District — an opportunity zone project touted by Albert — went up in an area with little else, as the program intended. Bounded on one side by the river and treetops of Anacostia Park and the other by crisscrossing roadways, the closest major development visible from the roof is the Marine One hangar about two miles away.

Albert credits D.C.’s expansive tax incentives for developers beyond opportunity zones. There’s the federal New Markets Tax Credit Program, the District’s low-income-housing tax credit, and even a local tax incentive for opening grocery stores.

“It's surpassed our expectations,” Albert said of opportunity zones. “I wouldn't say it's our premier tool.”

RedBrick LMD managing partner Louis Dubin had a different take.

“Anything we may have done locally would be so de minimis it would really not have materially contributed. So I would attribute this all to opportunity zone,” the real-estate developer told NOTUS.

entries.title: Lutnick Apologizes for Saying No U.S. Troops Have Died in the Iran War
entries.summary: He claimed to have “misspoke” after confusing the conflict with another U.S. operation in Venezuela.
entries.content:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick apologized Thursday for saying in an interview that no American service members have died supporting military operations in Iran, claiming that he “misspoke” and accidentally conflated the conflict with another U.S. operation in Venezuela.

Lutnick incorrectly stated the death toll during a CNBC appearance Wednesday, saying, “The way the president is playing Iran — there haven't been American deaths, it's really just an economic choke out.”

At least 18 service members have died and more than 400 troops have been wounded in action as the military campaign in Iran stretches into six months with no clear end in sight. The Pentagon has reclassified the deaths of four service members, all of whom were killed during an Iranian ballistic missile attack in Jordan in late July, as part of “overseas operations” instead of Operation Epic Fury, the military’s name for the initial conflict with Iran.

Lutnick clarified in a post to X Thursday he was thinking about the military operation in January to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, which reportedly injured seven American troops and killed about 100 Venezuelans.

“18 members of our military have died, and to those families my heart breaks and I am so very sorry for their loss,” Lutnick wrote of the Iran war. “As the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches, I am deeply thankful for our military and the sacrifices the men and women who serve our great country make, so such an attack, where I lost my brother Gary (36), my best friend Doug (39) and 656 other close friends and colleagues in the attacks on the World Trade Center, never happens again. Never!”

President Donald Trump also issued a clarification on Lutnick’s behalf Thursday.

“Sec. Lutnick had Venezuela on his mind when he said nobody was killed,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “18 people were killed in Iran!”

entries.title: Trump Says He’s Reconsidering His Support for UK Control Over the Falkland Islands
entries.summary: The president suggested that the UK’s lack of assistance during his war with Iran has made him think twice about supporting Britain’s claim to the territory.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump hinted on Thursday that he is reconsidering U.S. support for the U.K.’s claim to the Falkland Islands because of the country’s lack of support for his war against Iran.

Trump told British news channel GB News that Washington might not back the U.K. if Argentina were to invade the islands.

“Your country was not there to help me,” Trump said in a clip of the interview released on Thursday, referencing his frustration over Britain’s refusal to back U.S. military operations in Iran.

The U.S. has historically been neutral in the conflict, although Washington supported Britain’s campaign to control the Islands following an invasion by Argentina in 1982. In a 2013 referendum, residents voted 99.8% to remain a British overseas territory.

Trump’s comments come after Argentinian President Javier Milei, who has a close relationship with Trump, has launched an effort to claim control of the islands, restarting a long-standing dispute with the U.K. over the territory.

“The Malvinas were, are, and will always be Argentine,” Milei wrote on X in April.

Trump has repeatedly signaled his frustration with England and NATO for a lack of support in his ongoing war in Iran.

In the interview, Trump maintained that the U.K. is “not doing very well” and suggested the country had been weakened by repeated closures of the Strait of Hormuz. He argued the U.K. is “not the same country it was” when it initially won control over the Falkland Islands.

“I asked your former leader, ‘Why didn't you send a couple of ships?’” Trump said of the U.K.’s response to his war against Iran. “He said we don't have any, and it was pretty sad, the whole thing. So NATO was not there, even though most of those countries get a big portion of their oil from there.”

Trump also told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday that the United States was reviewing its position on the islands. Those comments followed reporting by The Daily Telegraph that the Pentagon was reviewing the U.S. position on the islands in order to incentivize its NATO allies to up their defense spending commitments.

“I always review every position,” Trump said. “That’s just one of many.

entries.title: A Nationals Homestand Full of Agony and Hope
entries.summary: When a team becomes competitive again, as the Nats have, baseball regains its power to please.
entries.content:
The Washington Nationals homestand, just completed, illustrates in miniature a baseball fan’s experiences over a lifetime.

The Nats are roughly a .500 team. That’s the talent level you’d expect if you were a fan from age 6 to 96. But, for 10 straight days, every game at Nats Park was experienced by ardent fans as either a joyous 1.000, full of promise, or an abysmal .000 that, at least for a while, feels almost unendurable.

On some recent days, fans could hardly get higher about their team’s future. On some days, often the next day, they could hardly feel worse.

During this fortnight, the Nats won a game 13-3. Laughers are fun. They also got a walk-off win on a Dylan Crews hit. Drama works nicely, too.

Daylen Lile won National League Player of the Week, then hit two more homers to start his next week —14 RBIs in eight games! Cade Cavalli, the team's new ace, had his ninth straight quality start, second-most in team history after only Max Scherzer’s streak in 2019.

On Tuesday, rookies Yoyo Morales and Jared Simpson were the hitting hero and winning pitcher on their first day in the majors. The Morales and Simpson families were sitting together in Nats Park. Morales had a homer, a long double and a single. Simpson got nine outs on the eight batters that he faced. The moms and dads hardly knew who to high-five next.

My favorite feel-good of the season is now lefty reliever Erik Tolman, who touched 100 mph with a 0.00 ERA in his first four Nats games after five years of misfortunes that’d make Job feel lucky by comparison. Two Tommy John surgeries were his little injuries.

In the minors in ’23, making his second TJ comeback, Tolman hopped over the foul line for luck, but caught his cleat and fell awkwardly.

“I tore every ligament in my [right] knee, [my] hamstring tore off my bone, and then the peroneal nerve ruptured,” said Tolman in a TV interview. “I lost all feeling in my foot, which resulted in a foot drop.”

Tolman had to learn how to walk again. He now pitches with a brace on his lower leg and, when barefoot, still doesn’t have full feeling in his foot. But his fastball sits at 96-to-99. On a foul pop up, Tolman made an acrobatic twisting snag, reaching backward over his head. Did somebody say the Nats needed a left-handed reliever more than any other one thing?

So, top that! What can go wrong?

Plenty. Baseball gives you a day to enjoy a Tolman, or a seven-inning, one-run 106-pitch outing by another southpaw rookie, Jackson Kent. But you also get just one day to rehab from the ugliest losses.

On Sunday, the Nats bullpen turned a 2-0 lead in the ninth into a 6-2 loss. The gruesome way that they did it shows why baseball fans deserve medals. Miami took a 4-2 lead on a bunt single, three walks, a hit batter, two double steals (one of home plate), a wild outfield throw on a sacrifice fly and multiple mental errors. The Marlins’ only “hit” had gone 10 feet in the air. But the next Miami hitter compensated for that distance disparity with a 400-foot home run.

George Solomon, the Washington Post's great sports editor for 28 years, emailed me: “Nats ninth inning performance Sunday as low as you can get.”

When a team blows its 35th save of the year, and the blown-save record, at least for this solar system, is only 37, a fan learns to root in the fetal position.

On a roller-coaster homestand as crazy as this, even rookie managers with cherubic faces get crusty. After one lazy 13-1 loss, Blake Butera publicly threw his team under the bus — where they deserved to be. His accusation of “lack of energy” is one step from “quit.”

Twice, Butera relieved Jake Irvin in the fifth inning before he was eligible for a win. It was the percentage move. Vets seldom like that; good managers don’t care. Butera also yanked Jorbit Vivas out mid-game for not running out a pop up. It would have been a waste for this season to be so cuddly that a ticked-off Butera never showed up.
Blake Butera (5702x3801, AR: 1.50)In other sports, devoted fans may wait a week for real news, or at least a few days. In MLB, the full range of a team’s possible futures rush at you constantly.

For example, with his current torrid streak, Lile now has a career OPS+ — OPS adjusted for era and home park — of 115, or 15% better than league average, in 929 plate appearances. Lile isn’t James Wood: 136! But 115 is in the same neighborhood as Ryan Zimmerman, Adrian Beltré, Roberto Alomar, Barry Larkin, Mickey Vernon, Thurman Munson and Byron Buxton. And Lile is only 23.

Counterbalancing that, Crews now has a .215 batting average in more than 800 plate appearances. After his walk-off hit, teammates pounded his back with joy because he’s such a hard-working, hard-nosed but hard-on-himself player who expects greatness — not mere goodness, much less mediocrity — from himself.

Take a deep breath. The average No. 2 overall draft pick has a career WAR of 15.2, not 50.0, and, if he’s an outfielder like Crews, a career average of 199 homers, not 500.

Useful centerfielder B.J. Upton (16.5 WAR, 168 homers), who was never an All-Star, is a fair measuring stick for a player in Crews’ draft slot, not Reggie Jackson. Crews has climbing to do, but reaching the top of a hill, not an Alp, might suffice.

As this season winds down, let’s step back. In recent years, the Nats have been almost unwatchable, even for a lunatic like me. This year, the fact that a late-season homestand could be engrossing proves how much progress the Paul Toboni regime has made.

You play for the scoreboard every day. But, over a season, your run differential tells plenty of truth, too. In ’26, the Nats have improved from -214 (awful) to +14 (average). That’s enormous.

Once a team becomes competitive again, as the Nats have, the sport regains its power to please. In one homestand near the end of a typical season for a typical team, so many remarkable things happen that a MLB fan can hardly believe it all, pulling out hair one night, but waking up smiling after the next game.

It’s 13-3 your way one night and a 13-1 loss two days later. This whole Nats homestand was a useful 6-4, with plenty of young players to ponder for the future. But in the final game Wednesday, the first-place Braves, kicked the previous night by those rookies, kicked back with a 9-0 win. The Nats got two hits.

After many years, you know this is how it goes. You internalize a coping mechanism for loss and an endless anticipation of hope. That sounds like daily existence. Recuperate and repeat. For a lifetime.

entries.title: Rep. Nikki Budzinski Announces a Bid to Chair the New Democrat Coalition
entries.summary: The Illinois representative wants to lead the centrist group as a slate of progressives are expected to enter Congress next year.
entries.content:
Rep. Nikki Budzinski wants to lead the centrist New Democrat Coalition next year, coinciding with an expected incoming wave of new House progressives hoping to expand the chamber’s left flank.

“I am confident I can lead us into what will be a consequential next chapter,” Budzinski said in a “Dear Colleague” letter seeking the group’s chairmanship, shared first with NOTUS.

Budzinski, a moderate who currently serves as the coalition’s vice chair of policy, is the first Democrat to throw her hat in the ring for the position.

With the likely arrival of a slate of new left-wing House Democrats, the party’s largest ideological caucus could face an uphill battle getting centrist priorities past the finish line even if Democrats win back the majority in November. Whoever chairs the group next year would need to balance potential conflicts between the party’s centrist and progressive wings.

In June, the group’s current chair, Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Illinois), waved away concerns about the way party priorities might shift next year.

“We’re not going to change who we are and what we’re fighting for,” Schneider, who is term-limited, told reporters. “You only do things by building a coalition, getting 218 votes. … Much of the legislative ideas we have put forth in the past and are proposing in the future are ideas that build coalitions that cross party lines.”

In her letter, Budzinski pointed to the party’s recent “commitment to pragmatic progress” and touted her work “toward building the largest majority possible.” The Illinois representative referenced her raising $2.5 million for House Democrats’ campaign arm this cycle and nearly $700,000 in direct contributions to “Red to Blue” candidates endorsed by the New Democrat Coalition’s political operation.

“Nikki has been a true leader who knows how to build a strong coalition that knows how to accomplish an agenda that moves this country forward,” Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nevada), a coalition member, told NOTUS. “She understands that in order for Democrats to hold a majority in Congress we must deliver results. I believe she will help do that.”

The elections for the New Democrat Coalition’s leadership for next the Congress will take place in November during new member orientation. It’s unclear if other lawmakers are considering running, but only current and former vice chairs can do so. Rep. Ami Bera (D-California), a former vice chair, previously considered a bid but his office confirmed he will not be running for next cycle.

entries.title: Maine Labor Day Rally Nixes Its Planned Graham Platner Speech
entries.summary: Platner had been scheduled to speak Monday at the rally in Ellsworth.
entries.content:
By Patrick Whittle

PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Former Democratic Senate nominee Graham Platner is no longer set to speak at a Labor Day rally when he makes his first major public appearance since ending his campaign against Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine.

Platner, who won the nomination in June but dropped out in July after Politico reported that a former girlfriend said he sexually assaulted her, had been scheduled to speak Monday at the rally in Ellsworth, near his hometown of Sullivan. He has denied the allegations.

Platner was expected to speak about labor history and the importance of unions in the U.S. Event organizers were urged not to let him speak by the former girlfriend and another woman who has accused him of domestic abuse.

Organizers said Wednesday that the planned speech was drawing negative media attention, and he will instead lead a veterans' march after the rally.

“Graham is not speaking,” said Carol Leonard of Hancock County Activists, a progressive group organizing the rally. “The media frenzy got just too insane, and we became concerned about safety.”

Platner is an oyster farmer and combat veteran who filled theaters around Maine during a barnstorming campaign that resulted in a decisive win over Gov. Janet Mills, who suspended her campaign before the primary.

He has no experience in elected office but fashioned a campaign focused on working-class issues such as the high costs of housing and healthcare.

Platner’s campaign was frequently interrupted by scandals, such as the emergence in late May of media reports that he previously exchanged sexually explicit text messages with several women while he was married.

High-profile backers including independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders stood by him in the wake of those allegations, but his support crumbled after the sexual assault allegations surfaced.

Platner also had a tattoo recognized as a Nazi symbol, though he said he did not realize its association with Nazism until he was several weeks into the campaign. He later had the tattoo covered up with a different design.

Platner also apologized for old online comments that included insulting language about women, police and rural residents.

After he dropped out of the race, Democrats held a nominating convention in July in which they chose former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson to run against Collins.

Jackson, who got the Senate nomination after losing a gubernatorial primary, campaigned with Platner in the spring but has distanced himself from him following the sexual assault allegations.

The Ellsworth event is scheduled for midday and will include speakers, live music and the veterans' march.

entries.title: Fox Abruptly Parts Ways With Longtime Host Maria Bartiromo
entries.summary: The conservative media company did not specify a reason for the separation.
entries.content:
FOX News Media announced Thursday that its host, Maria Bartiromo, is no longer with the company after more than 12 years.

“We thank Maria for her work,” a statement read, “and wish her all the best on her next chapter.”

The statement did not specify the reasons for the separation.

Bartiromo hosted “Mornings with Maria” that aired on FOX Business Network, the last episode of which aired Thursday morning, as well as “Maria Bartiromo's Wall Street.”

entries.title: The Pentagon ‘Temporarily’ Rescinds Its New Testosterone Screening Guidance
entries.summary: The clinical guidance published yesterday by the Defense Health Agency has now been removed from its website to “allow for updates.”
entries.content:
The Pentagon has “temporarily rescinded” the clinical guidance draft published Wednesday detailing its new testosterone screening policy for service members.

The document was removed from the Defense Health Agency’s website, as first reported by Reuters, though the interim guidance still remains in place, a Department of Defense official told NOTUS.

“The draft ‘Clinical Guidance for Health and Human Performance Optimization’ published on September 2, 2026, has been temporarily rescinded to allow for updates,” the official said.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the mandatory testosterone screening policy in July, saying the new guidance would apply to all service members 30 and older. Service members under the age of 30 could also voluntarily request to have the screenings.

The screenings would be conducted during the service members’ periodic health assessments, which are required annually.

“This initiative is not about artificial enhancement,” Hegseth said in a video posted to X on July 15. “It’s about restoring and optimizing your natural capabilities, protecting your longevity and ensuring you have the biological foundation required to sustain and fight.”

Testosterone levels naturally drop about 1% a year for men, beginning in their late 30s, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

entries.title: ICE Officer Accused of Lying to Investigators About Minnesota Shooting
entries.summary: Christian Castro, the officer who authorities say shot a Venezuelan man in the leg, has been charged with making false statements to federal investigators.
entries.content:
By Alanna Durkin Richer

Federal prosecutors have charged a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with lying to investigators about the events leading up to the shooting of a Venezuelan man during the Minneapolis immigration crackdown earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.

The person was not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke on condition of anonymity. The person said Christian Castro, the officer who authorities say shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg in January, has been charged with making false statements to federal investigators.

The federal charges follow Castro's release from jail last week after Texas’ governor refused to immediately sign an extradition warrant to hand him over to Minnesota authorities, who have charged him separately with assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.

Federal authorities had initially accused Sosa-Celis and another man of beating an officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel during the confrontation. But federal prosecutors dropped charges against the men after video evidence showed the officers may have lied about the encounter, and officials opened an investigation.

entries.title: Trump Administration Escalates Its Anti-DEI Push at Universities
entries.summary: The administration is seeking to strip tax-exempt status for private schools and colleges over their DEI policies.
entries.content:
By Collin Binkley

The Trump administration is proposing a new rule that would strip private schools and colleges of their tax-exempt status if they provide targeted help to students based on their race, a significant escalation in the White House's campaign to eradicate diversity programs directed at Black, Hispanic and other minority students.

The Treasury Department proposed the change Thursday in a new regulation that, if made final, would kick in after May 2027. The rule is broadly aimed at ending any policies or programs that help students because of their race, and it specifically says such benefits in admissions, scholarships and facilities “would be incompatible” with the rule.

It’s the latest attempt by the Trump administration to pressure schools and colleges to weed out diversity, equity and inclusion policies that had become common before President Donald Trump returned to the White House with a promise to end them. Trump officials have used Civil Rights-era laws to unwind the policies, saying they discriminate against white and Asian American students.

Scores of universities have shut down or rebranded their DEI offices and ended scholarships and clubs designed for minority students under pressure from the White House. In a statement announcing the proposal, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested that even policies that are no longer under the banner of DEI could be targeted.

“Schools rebranding race-based preferences as equitable, inclusive, or diversity-enhancing does not change their discriminatory nature,” Bessent said.

The Treasury Department and IRS estimate that up to 18,000 private schools, colleges and other education institutions could be affected by the proposal.

America’s private universities have been exempt from many taxes for more than a century because they provide a public good. The benefit saves many universities millions of dollars every year.

Trump has seen the tax-exempt status as a lever to pull in his pressure campaign against colleges that he describes as hotbeds of “wokeness.” He threatened to cut the benefit for Harvard University last year during his battle with the nation’s oldest college. In a response, Harvard officials said there was no legal basis for doing so and argued it would force cuts to financial aid and crucial medical research.

It’s incredibly rare for the federal government to go after a college’s tax-exempt status, but there’s one notable precedent. Bob Jones University, a small Christian school in South Carolina, lost the benefit in the 1970s over a ban on interracial dating and marriage on campus. The Supreme Court upheld the IRS’s decision to deny the school its exemption. The school has since ended the ban and regained tax-exempt status in 2017.

Laws forbid the IRS from targeting individuals and organizations for ideological reasons, and federal officials are not allowed to direct IRS investigations.

To maintain nonprofit status, which allows donations to be tax-deductible, organizations must follow IRS rules on lobbying, political campaign activity and annual reporting requirements, as well as other obligations.

The Trump administration describes the new proposal as a move toward restoring merit in the nation’s education systems.

The Justice Department has separately opened investigations into several medical schools that it accuses of favoring Black and Hispanic students in admissions. Trump officials say any such favoritism violates Title IV of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, a federal law that forbids discrimination in education and was created to fight segregation and its impact.

A statement from IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said private schools that promote discriminatory practices will no longer be exempt from taxes.

“Today’s proposed regulations put institutions on notice and schools that continue to engage in racial discrimination should expect to lose that status,” he said.

___

Associated Press Education Writer Annie Ma contributed to this report.

entries.title: House GOP Leadership Cancels Two Weeks of Votes Ahead of the Midterms
entries.summary: The chamber was originally scheduled to be in session for the full month of September.
entries.content:
House Republican leadership canceled the last two weeks of September votes on Thursday, meaning that after members depart the Capitol later this month they will not return until after the November midterm election.

“This is a change from House GOP leadership’s previously announced schedule,” Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Massachusetts) wrote in an update.

House lawmakers are now set to leave Washington on Sept. 17 rather than Oct. 1 for their break before the midterm elections.

The official House legislative calendar, maintained by House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana), shows that the House was supposed to be in session the week of Sept. 21 and Sept. 28.

When House lawmakers came back to Washington earlier this week after a monthlong August recess, they quickly passed a stopgap measure to keep federal agencies funded until mid-December. The funding bill averts the threat of a government shutdown ahead of the midterm elections.

House Speaker Mike Johnson has frequently touted the 119th Congress as “one of the most productive Congresses in the history of the institution.”

But last year under Johnson’s speakership, Congress set a 21st-century record for casting the least amount of votes, according to The Washington Post. The 362 votes the chamber held was half as many votes as in 2017, which was the first year of President Donald Trump’s first term in office with a Republican majority.

With only a few months left of the year and more canceled in-session weeks on the horizon, the House has held less than 300 votes in 2026.

entries.title: Trump Asks the Supreme Court to Reinstate Mail-In Ballot Rules
entries.summary: A lower court stayed the Postal Service from implementing new rules on ballots ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to allow the U.S. Postal Service to enforce new mail ballot rules ahead of the November midterms.

The Justice Department petitioned the high court to lift a lower court’s temporary order blocking key parts of the rule enacted as part of a crackdown by the administration on mail-in ballots.

“The district court’s continued prejudgment of the rule is baseless, and an immediate stay is warranted,” Solicitor General John Sauer wrote.

The administration’s new policy requires local election officials to use only federally approved ballot envelopes. It also requires those officials to upload voters’ names, addresses and ballot barcodes to a Postal Service portal. Mailed ballots that do not meet those standards could be returned to election officials.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, an Obama appointee in Massachusetts, found last week that the states challenging the new rules were likely to show that the Postal Service exceeded its authority.

She said imposing the requirements weeks before ballots are mailed could prevent eligible voters from receiving them.

The Supreme Court has not ruled on the new request. 

This is a developing story and will be updated.

entries.title: Energy Jobs Fell in Almost Every Sector Last Year
entries.summary: The Energy Department found only that transmission, storage and distribution sectors grew, in part due to the expansion of data centers.
entries.content:
The energy industry’s workforce shrank last year.

The energy sector lost roughly 86,000 workers — roughly 1% of its workforce — between 2024 and 2025, according to an annual report from the Department of Energy. The losses came from almost every part of the energy industry, the United States Energy and Employment Report said, amid increased automation and the Trump administration’s push away from green energy.

Only the transmission, distribution and storage parts of the energy sector saw job growth in 2025, a trend DOE officials attributed to the expansion of data centers, growth in manufacturing and industrial activity and the increased adoption of electric vehicles and heat pumps. Enrollment in apprenticeship programs also increased.

The Trump administration’s efforts to increase coal- and nuclear-power generation led to employment bumps, with each of those industries adding about 2,500 workers.

But as a whole, the power-generation sector lost about 15,000 workers from 2024 to 2025. Most of those losses were in the solar industry, with additional job losses in wind and hydroelectric power.

Jobs in petroleum and natural gas also declined in 2025, dropping by 3% and 4%, respectively. Energy officials said that reflected a shift toward a “smaller, higher-paid workforce.”

“Industry sources also point out the role of AI, automation, and digital technologies in improving operational efficiencies and reducing labor requirements,” the report said.

About 50,000 jobs disappeared from the motor-vehicle industry in 2025, but wages in that sector also increased. Energy Department officials said “output-per-worker” increased over that time, too.

The report found that higher-wage occupations added workers in 2025, while lower-wage occupations declined. The median salary in the energy sector in 2025 was $63,000, higher than the national median of $51,000.

Across several energy industry sectors, employers reported having difficulty hiring workers and concerns about a lack of people available for technical positions like electric work or construction.

Despite the drop in employment, the Energy Department report projected that demand for workers in the energy sector would increase as electricity demand rises and data centers expand.

entries.title: A Democratic Reckoning on Data Centers Is Coming
entries.summary: The issue of limiting new facilities is becoming a central flashpoint in the midterms, but the top House Democrat is avoiding specifics.
entries.content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries could be on a collision course with progressives and grassroots activists who are demanding Congress pass legislation to pause the construction of new data centers. Jeffries, who is set to become speaker if his party wins the House majority in November, hasn’t weighed in on whether he will push a moratorium.

Polls show Americans have recoiled from President Donald Trump’s directive to become the “world’s No. 1 superpower in artificial intelligence” and the recent blitz of data centers. Democratic candidates across the country are campaigning on a pledge to pause or ban the construction of new data center projects.

Trump’s call this week to “let Data Reign” and his description of communities that oppose these facilities as “backwards and poor” gives Democrats an opening to contrast with Republicans on the ballot in November. Some Republicans have worked to distance themselves from the president on the issue, which is bubbling up in areas where new development is exploding.

Jeffries criticized a pair of House Republicans in purple districts over their votes to “unleash data centers on the American people in an unfettered fashionn— Reps. David Valadao of California and Mike Lawler of New York.

But while Valadao’s Democratic challenger has endorsed a one-year pause on data centers in his district, Jeffries and other House Democratic leaders remain skeptical of a ban.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), who has introduced a bill that would place an indefinite moratorium on data centers until Congress enacts safeguards, told NOTUS that voters are looking to lawmakers to address “the effects that AI and data centers are having in their lives.”

“Whether that is a moratorium, whether it is a pause, so that there’s actual consent in these communities on what is built, that’s what I think people want the most,” Ocasio-Cortez said.

Jeffries said this week that Americans “want some restraint so that they’re not overrun by the possibility of their electricity bills continuing to skyrocket and their water bills continuing to skyrocket.”

But the Democratic leader has pumped the brakes on a calling for a strict ban. He told Politico this summer that a moratorium is “not a position that I’ve articulated at this moment.” Rep. Frank Pallone (D-New Jersey), the top Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, supports a moratorium but has not committed to pushing one if he chairs the committee next year. Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Florida), the top Democrat on the panel’s energy subcommittee, opposes a moratorium.

Jeffries’ office declined a request from NOTUS to comment on his policy position.

Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vermont), a progressive who hasn’t taken a stance, told NOTUS that there are “competing interests” for the Democratic policy prescription on data centers.

“What (voters) are telling us is, we need to take a beat,” Balint said. “This needs to be a really thoughtfully rolled out plan.”

Mitch Jones, managing director of policy and litigation at Food and Water Watch, an environmental advocacy group that has pushed for a moratorium on new data centers, told NOTUS that Democratic leadership “hasn't really come to terms” with the grassroots energy behind the anti-data-center movement and what it means for AI policy in Washington.

“They're going to be caught off guard if they don't start paying attention to what's happening on the ground,” Jones said. “If they try to do some sort of squishy or milquetoast policy on AI or data centers, there will be an immediate backlash from their base.”

Jones said that embracing strict regulations is important for Democrats because it “sends a message to voters across the country that they're actually listening to them, not the Silicon Valley executives whose private jets” lawmakers fly on.

The push to rein in data centers isn’t just gaining traction on the campaign trail. More Democrats on the Hill are embracing the policy, and urging leadership for a vote on the issue in the future.

Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Massachusetts) told NOTUS that he thinks it’s important to go on the record to send a message.

“We ought to at least give members the opportunity to vote on the national moratorium,” McGovern said.

entries.title: This Minnesota Congressional Hopeful Is Trying to Break the World Handshake Record
entries.summary: Matt Little will take on a big challenge Saturday when he attempts to beat the two-decade-old record.
entries.content:
You have to hand it to him.

Minnesota congressional candidate Matt Little is eyeing an ambitious goal this week: More than 13,000 handshakes in eight hours, which would be a new world record.

He said it’s been on his mind for more than a decade: a record so untouched it has only been held by two other people, an influential governor and one of the nation’s most formative presidents.

Little will need to break the late New Mexico Gov. Bill Richardson’s Guinness World Record for most handshakes by a politician, which he achieved in 2002 by shaking 13,392 hands in just eight hours, besting President Theodore Roosevelt’s previous mark of 8,513.

Little, who beat a crowded primary field to become the Democratic nominee for Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District, will take on the challenge Saturday at the Minnesota State Fair.

“I like competitive activities but I also love shaking hands,” Little said in an interview with NOTUS on Thursday. “I do think that is the foundational building block of our democracy, like the Constitution, is a written handshake, right? In these times too, we've got to get back to that. I believe very strongly the things I believe in, and I'm willing to have that conversation with anybody, even if we're diametrically opposed.”

Not that there will be much time for talking — to reach the world record, Little estimates that he’ll have to average a whopping 29 handshakes a minute.

The progressive and former state senator said he is also pursuing this big challenge because he wants to bring the record “home to Minnesota.” Little is currently running against Republican state Sen. Eric Pratt to succeed Rep. Angie Craig, who lost a Senate primary last month to Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan.

To prepare for Saturday’s event, Little told NOTUS he has been training for weeks with a hand-gripper exercise tool to build strength. He stopped doing his regular exercise routine, which usually consists of push-ups and pull-ups, on Wednesday because “we don't want any injuries or pulled muscles heading into Saturday morning.”

When asked if he was serious about pausing physical activity ahead of Saturday’s record-breaking attempt, Little replied, “I’m, as the kids say these days, deadass.”

Little estimated his current personal best is the 1,000 hands he shook during a parade this year.

On Saturday, Little plans to begin his journey at the booth for the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party. If the attendance slows down, Little said he will pivot to seeking out the state fair’s longest lines, where his campaign staff will tell eventgoers, “There's gonna be a guy coming by trying to shake as many hands to break a world record, we'd love you to participate.”

Little’s staff will keep track using clickers. They will also film the event and upload it to YouTube for verification purposes.

As for how he plans to avoid germs, Little said there will be plenty of hand sanitizer on hand for both himself and those who shake his hand.

“Every handshake is unique, and it's never the same experience twice,” he said. “I'm gonna give it my all.”

entries.title: Trump Says There’s a ‘War’ With Iran. Vance Says There’s Not.
entries.summary: President Trump has expressed continued confidence that the conflict will end soon, while Vance says he wouldn’t “set an artificial timeline.”
entries.content:
Vice President JD Vance downplayed the U.S.’s conflict with Iran on Thursday, saying he “wouldn’t call it a war” — contrasting President Donald Trump’s ongoing references to a “war that we’re easily winning.”

“The phrase ‘an end to the war,’ I want to push back on that just a little bit because major combat operations are currently not ongoing, and they haven't been ongoing in a very long time,” Vance said while hosting the White House press briefing Thursday.

When asked about when the monthslong war might end, Vance told reporters he can’t provide an “artificial timeline” should Iranians “start blowing up oil and gas ships” after that hypothetical deadline.

“It would be irresponsible for us to write out our strategy and our timeline for an Iranian nation that simply cannot honor its commitments and cannot stop shooting at commercial ships,” Vance said.

Trump has adopted a much different posture to describe the ongoing hostilities with Iran. The president has continued to call it a “war” when speaking to reporters and posting about the conflict on Truth Social.

In a post just hours before Vance’s briefing, Trump called the conflict a war as he criticized the media for reporting on depleted munitions stockpiles putting a strain on combat operations in the Middle East, which the White House has vehemently denied.

“The people and Media Outlets that keep harping on the fact that we have no ammunition (And they are 100% wrong!), are actually treasonous. They do it because they would rather see the United States LOSE a War that we’re easily WINNING,” Trump wrote Thursday on Truth Social.

While Vance says an end to the conflict depends on Iran’s action, Trump has continued to express confidence that the war is “going to end pretty soon,” suggesting this week that the most recent exchange of fire between the U.S. and Iran won’t last “too long.”

The U.S. resumed major strikes against Iran this week and targeted assets in the Strait of Hormuz. Trump threatened Iran with the “biggest attack of them all,” but the country still launched retaliatory strikes on the U.S.’s regional allies, including Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait.

The Strait of Hormuz has remained a critical juncture throughout the conflict because a significant amount of the global oil supply passes through it. As Vance noted Thursday, Iran has been able to have a substantial “effect on world energy markets” by targeting commercial shipping vessels.

The U.S. has maintained a heavy naval presence in the strait. Trump floated renaming the waterway “Trump Strait” on Wednesday on Truth Social, though he later said he was “just throwing that out.”

entries.title: Lev Parnas Used Congressional Campaign Funds to Pay Cleaning Company, Makeup Artist
entries.summary: Parnas’ campaign told regulators it paid the Florida companies for “PR services” and “strategy consulting.”
entries.content:
Lev Parnas’ Florida congressional campaign paid a cleaning company and makeup artist thousands of dollars for services they don’t appear to provide — raising questions about whether funds were used for personal expenses.

The campaign of Parnas — a former Rudy Giuliani ally sentenced to prison earlier this decade in part for campaign finance crimes — disclosed paying $18,500 in April to Hands at Work LLC for “PR Services,” according to FEC records.

Hands at Work LLC is a cleaning company, according to a man who identified himself as the son of Marelbi Franco, who is listed as the company manager on Florida business records, when contacted by NOTUS. Franco’s son ended the call after NOTUS asked what PR services the Parnas campaign had paid the cleaning company to handle.

The Parnas campaign’s address is a mailbox at a UPS store in Miami, and the campaign has not disclosed in its FEC reports ever paying for physical campaign office space.

The Parnas campaign also paid $3,000 in May to Le Tropique Inc. for “strategy consulting,” according to its latest FEC report. Le Tropique Inc. is a Florida-based makeup studio owned by Terry Jacobs, who did not respond to an email or phone call requesting comment.

Most of the $30,000 Parnas’ campaign committee has raised through June went to services from Hands at Work LLC and Le Tropique Inc., according to FEC records.

Federal campaign finance law prohibits the use of campaign funds for personal expenses.

Neither the Parnas campaign nor campaign treasurer Andrew Madras responded to repeated requests for comment. NOTUS tried several phone numbers for Parnas and eventually reached a person who identified themself as one of Parnas’ representatives. The person, who did not offer their name, declined to provide Parnas’ contact information but said they would pass on NOTUS’ inquiry.

On Tuesday, Parnas told his 82,000 Substack subscribers that his “campaign is real” and warned there was “a coordinated effort to disrupt our community by spreading lies and misinformation about me and my campaign.”

“As I have been warning you, organized disinformation campaigns are being carried out by paid actors whose goal is to discredit, divide, and disrupt our community,” Parnas wrote. “That is why facts matter. That is why transparency matters. And that is why I will always show you the receipts.”

A key figure in President Donald Trump’s first impeachment trial, Parnas has rebranded himself as an anti-Trump crusader and built a sizable social media following — although his online presence pales in comparison to that of his son, Aaron Parnas, a prominent Democratic influencer and news aggregator who has more than 5 million TikTok followers.

The elder Parnas’ entry in electoral politics this year had proven decidedly turbulent.

Parnas initially filed to run as a Democrat in Florida’s 27th Congressional District, currently held by Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar. He then amended his federal election paperwork in June to run as an independent in Florida’s 22nd Congressional District, which leans Republican, according to the nonpartisan election handicappers at the Cook Political Report.

“I helped build MAGA, and now I promise you I will do everything in my power to dismantle the corruption surrounding it piece by piece, truth by truth, until democracy wins,” Parnas said in a video on his Subtack announcing his campaign.

At present, Parnas’ name does not appear on the Florida Division of Elections’ list of congressional candidates, as independent journalist Troy Barile first noted on Medium.

The Florida Division of Elections did not respond to emails from NOTUS asking if Parnas’ name will appear on the 22nd Congressional District’s general election ballot. Parnas’ campaign has not spent any money on traditional political advertising, according to the ad tracking platform AdImpact. Parnas personally posts frequently on his YouTube page, including a recent interview with Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden.

Parnas burst into the national spotlight during Trump’s first impeachment trial, where Trump faced charges of abuse of power and obstruction of justice. Parnas, who was born in Ukraine, alleged Giuliani sent him to urge the Ukrainian government to open an investigation into the Bidens ahead of the 2020 presidential election — and that Trump “knew exactly what was going on,” an allegation Trump has denied.

In 2021, a jury convicted Parnas of campaign finance crimes, among others, for conspiring to funnel money from a Russian oligarch into U.S. elections. He was sentenced in 2022 to 20 months in prison and was released in September 2023, according to the Bureau of Prisons’ inmate database.

Parnas and Hunter Biden reconciled after his release. During his interview with the younger Biden, which was released last week on Kick, Parnas again apologized to the entire Biden family.

“What we’re seeing play out in Trump 2.0 is the sicker we could get, the more crazier we could do it, the more sycophantic we could become,” Parnas said, adding, “It’s just incredible to watch, man.”

entries.title: Swing-State Republicans Are Skipping Trump’s Midterm Convention
entries.summary: With 60 days until the midterms, many lawmakers are forgoing the event, dubbed “Trumpapalooza,” to campaign.
entries.content:
An increasing number of Republicans say they plan to skip President Donald Trump’s midterm convention next week in Dallas, which has been dubbed “Trumpapalooza” by the Republican National Committee.

The convention, which is set to kick off on Wednesday, carries a high price tag for lawmakers, with House members reportedly expected to contribute $25,000 each to attend. And it’s unclear whether attending a spectacle revolving around Trump will be beneficial for those Republicans locked in tight midterm contests after the president’s approval rating hit record lows last month.

Sen. Mike Rounds, who’s up for reelection in South Dakota, told reporters earlier this week that he plans to skip the event because he’s meeting with constituents across his state.

“That’s up to the folks that want to put it on,” Rounds said when asked if it’s a good idea for Republicans to put on a multimillion-dollar spectacle while voters grapple with rising costs. “This year, I’m spending as much time as I can in South Dakota talking to folks that do have concerns. Affordability is one of them.”

Trump is set to headline the two-day event, with Vice President JD Vance also slated to speak. Most top Republican leaders, including Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune, will attend the convention.

But other Republican lawmakers have cited a variety of reasons for sitting out. Some had already planned to campaign in their districts, while others blamed fundraisers or family events. Trump did not announce the dates of the convention until late June.

Reps. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), Tom Barrett (R-Michigan) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pennsylvania) are all running in races the Cook Political Report have deemed “toss ups.” With just 60 days until the midterm elections, all three told Politico this week they don’t plan to attend the convention.

Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor in Wisconsin, also told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that he’s planning to skip the event. And embattled Rep. Max Miller of Ohio, who has been accused of abusing his ex-wife and daughter, told The New York Times he’ll also stay home.

But other Republicans who are facing difficult reelection bids are planning to travel to Dallas next week. Former Rep. Mike Rogers, who’s running for an open Senate seat in Michigan, Sen. Jon Husted, who’s defending his Ohio Senate seat, and Rep. Scott Perry, who’s facing a tough race in Pennsylvania, are all slated to attend.

Johnson told reporters on Tuesday that he’s been promoting the event “everywhere I’ve been,” but acknowledged there are likely to be some absences in the Republican conference.

“Some of them need to be in the district on those two days, Sept. 9 and 10,” Johnson said. “It’s a critical time right before early voting begins nationwide. So people made individual decisions based on what’s best for their districts and all.”

Vance also said that he didn’t have concerns about congressional absences at the event, telling reporters that “we don't need a congressman in a tight race to be there in all cases.”

“Sometimes it might be better if that guy's out there raising money,” Vance said. “What we want is every person in a tight race to go out there and make the best case they can to their constituents, so they can get reelected, and so we can do more good for the American people. That's the goal.”

Still, staunch supporters of the president in safe seats are also planning to avoid the convention. Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, who leads the House Oversight Committee, said he will be in his home state during the House’s previously scheduled recess next week.

“I had stuff already planned in my congressional district or I would be there, but I got a lot going on back in Kentucky,” Comer said in an interview with NewsNation. “My time is needed there … I don’t think most members of Congress are on a regular schedule to go to party conventions.”

And Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar told CNN that she’ll be in her South Florida district during the festivities.

“I have to be in the district because I have events,” Salazar said. “I would love to go. I was thinking about it. I’m going to miss out on something important, but I cannot be in two places at the same time.”

entries.title: Leon Black Sues to Block House Subpoenas Over His Epstein Ties
entries.summary: The House oversight panel’s ranking Democrat said the billionaire investor should be held in contempt for skipping sworn testimony Thursday.
entries.content:
Billionaire investor Leon Black, who was closely associated with Jeffrey Epstein, sued the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee on Thursday, seeking to block subpoenas in the panel’s investigation of the late sex offender’s network.

Black did not show up for a scheduled deposition before the committee Thursday morning, and instead challenged two subpoenas: one that sought nondisclosure agreements that Black may have been party to, and another that compelled him to testify before the committee.

The committee issued the subpoenas after Black voluntarily sat for an interview about his relationship with Epstein but refused to answer what lawmakers said were key questions. Epstein served for years as a paid financial adviser to Black.

In the lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, Black alleges the subpoenas issued in June are invalid and says they seek private information that has no “legitimate connection” to the committee’s work.

Black has already testified to Congress that Epstein had nothing to do with drafting or creating any confidentiality agreements he may possess, the lawsuit says, and the subpoena compels production of “a vast quantity of agreements of all kinds.”

It also argues the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee.”

The 28-page complaint, which names the House oversight committee and Chair James Comer as defendants, seeks a court order barring the panel from enforcing the subpoenas. It argues the subpoenas are overbroad and exceed the committee’s authority.

In a statement Thursday morning, Comer sharply criticized Black for refusing to appear for his deposition and for filing the lawsuit.

“It’s a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people,” Comer said. “Mr. Black’s testimony is crucial to our investigation as he was one of Mr. Epstein’s fee paying clients and has several nondisclosure agreements.”

Comer added that the deposition would move forward with an empty chair for Black, and that he would discuss next steps with committee members.

The committee’s top Democrat, Rep. Robert Garcia, said Thursday that Black must be held in contempt of Congress. He accused Black of having “funded Epstein's abuse and trafficking of women,” saying Black had paid Epstein tens of millions of dollars over several years.

"The process of contempt has to begin. It is not acceptable that he's not coming in, and his lawsuit against the committee is laughable," Garcia told reporters at the Capitol.

A lawyer for Black didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The committee is probing federal authorities’ handling of their investigation into Epstein and his accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell, for trafficking and sexually abusing girls and women. Lawmakers are also examining the pair’s ties to a broad network of powerful and wealthy business leaders, government officials and academics.

Black, who made his fortune working in private equity, stepped down from his role leading Apollo Global Management in 2021 amid scrutiny of his ties to Epstein. His name appears hundreds of times in the millions of investigative files that Congress forced the Justice Department to release last year. Survivors of Epstein’s abuse have called for the Justice Department to investigate him.

Lawmakers on the oversight committee voiced frustration with Black’s June 26 interview, with Republicans and Democrats saying at the time that he had refused to answer “vital” questions. Comer and Garcia said NDAs that Black allegedly signed with women were essential to the committee’s investigation and that it was critical to find out whether Epstein was involved.

The committee’s inquiry into the documents was “directly relevant to understanding the operation of sex-trafficking rings, potential impediments to the federal government’s investigations of sex-trafficking rings, and the potential methods for Mr. Epstein and Ms. Maxwell to exercise influence over associates to protect their illegal activities,” Comer wrote in a letter attached to the subpoena.

In general, nondisclosure agreements do not protect criminal activity.

Epstein died in federal custody in 2019 after being charged with federal sex-trafficking crimes. Authorities ruled it a suicide. Maxwell is serving a 20-year sentence in federal prison after being convicted of helping him groom, traffic and abuse minors.

entries.title: Trump Names New Acting Army Secretary After Tension-Filled Resignation
entries.summary: Adam Telle, assistant secretary of the Army for civil works, will take over as civilian Army leader.
entries.content:
By Jonathan J. Cooper and Ben Finley

President Donald Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle as the acting Army secretary following the departure of Dan Driscoll amid widespread reports of tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Telle is currently the assistant secretary of the Army for civil works.

“He is a Great Patriot, who is respected by all,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

Driscoll gave no explanation for his decision to quit this week as the Army's top civilian official. His clashes with Hegseth have been widely reported, and some of Driscoll’s allies in the Army were ousted this year by Trump’s Pentagon chief.

Telle has been at the Army Office of Civil Works since August 2025, according to Legistorm, a website that tracks lawmakers and Capitol Hill staffers. Before that, Telle spent 20 years mostly working in Congress for lawmakers, including as chief of staff for Republican Sen. Bill Haggerty of Tennessee from 2021 to 2025.

Telle had a job for 18 months working in the White House during Trump's first term as a special assistant to the president for legislative affairs, Legistorm said. He also spent more than 10 years working for the late Republican Sen. Thad Cochran of Mississippi.

Telle will be overseeing the nation’s largest fighting force at a time when the U.S. is still engaged in conflict with Iran and significant Army forces are stationed in the Middle East.

The war has significantly contributed to the U.S. military’s shortfall in critical weapons like the Patriot and THAAD defense missile interceptors systems, which are operated by the Army.

Driscoll, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, did not offer an explanation for why he stepped down after 18 months as the service’s civilian leader.

He is a friend of Vice President JD Vance and had good relationships with both Republicans and Democrats in Congress. His allies in the Army who were ousted by Hegseth included its top uniformed leader, Gen. Randy George.

Gen. Christopher LaNeve took over as the Army’s acting chief of staff and recently pulled the plug on a drone modernization program that Driscoll had championed.

Driscoll spoke with Trump on the current state of the Army before he submitted his resignation, The Associated Press has reported.

Driscoll did not allude to any problems in the only public statement on his departure, saying Tuesday that it has been “the honor of a lifetime” to serve as Army secretary under Trump and Hegseth.

“We could not have made the progress we did without the support of Secretary Hegseth,” he added.

Democrats and Republicans lamented Driscoll’s departure, with some blaming Hegseth directly.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who is retiring and sometimes has clashed with Trump, said on social media that Hegseth “is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks.”
