entries.title: Missouri Supreme Court Blocks GOP Redistricting Map
entries.summary: The state attorney general said she would appeal the ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court.
entries.content:
The Missouri Supreme Court on Thursday blocked the state from continuing to use Republicans’ redrawn congressional map and allowed a November ballot referendum on the issue to move forward.

The ruling to block Republicans’ new map breaks from other redistricting cases this year in red states, where gerrymandering efforts have generally withstood more legal challenges than in Democratic ones.

“What we got today is not an easy accomplishment,” Richard von Glaghn, the executive director of nonprofit People Not Politicians, which sought a ballot referendum on the issue, said at a press conference shortly after the ruling. “It is a unanimous decision from the Supreme Court and it reaffirms what we have said all along. We have the right to do a referendum and a law cannot go into effect until the people decide.”

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway quickly said that she planned to appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court, saying that the Thursday decision disenfranchised Missouri voters.

President Donald Trump bemoaned the “horrible, ridiculous and unconstitutional” decision in a Truth Social post soon after the ruling, saying there isn’t “enough time to change the map back.” 

“Missouri must be able to use the map that was in effect just a couple of months ago, in the Primary,” Trump wrote. “This is a Dark Day for ‘Justice’ in Missouri!”

The state’s Republicans were among the first to take up President Donald Trump’s national call to redraw congressional maps to gain more U.S. House seats before the midterms. Lawmakers passed a map that was expected to give Republicans a 7-1 House advantage by drawing out Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s seat in Kansas City, slicing the district he has represented for over 20 years into three parts.

While Missouri’s new map was used in the August primaries, the state must employ the old 6-2 map for the upcoming midterms, the court ruled.

“The referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely, and the secretary incorrectly concluded otherwise,” Judge Ginger K. Gooch wrote in the 14-page opinion. “HB 1 did not go into effect and will not go into effect unless and until approved by the voters. The congressional redistricting the General Assembly established in 2022 remains in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election.”

The state constitution allows voters to force a referendum on laws passed by the general assembly. Shortly after lawmakers passed a new map last fall, People Not Politicians promptly filed a petition with over 330,000 signatures, more than double the necessary amount, to Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins. On Aug. 4, Hoskins, a Republican, blocked the referendum effort, a decision a circuit judge later upheld.

Missouri Supreme Court Chief Justice Brent Powell later that month urged lower court judges to move quickly on the case, citing a state law that restricts changing the ballot after Sept. 8. The high court on Wednesday heard two cases filed by People Not Politicians.

As he left the U.S. Capitol on his way back to Kansas City to await the ruling, Cleaver told NOTUS that the redistricting effort led by Republicans in his state was them putting “political advantage over everything.”

“They wanted to cheat,” Cleaver said on Wednesday. “The polling data shows that the people in Missouri overwhelmingly oppose this — Black, White, brown, Republican, Democrat, independent. Nobody thinks that this is wholesome for the community, but they don't care about that. The issue is, you know, the president wants the seats.”

Republicans have successfully redrawn their maps to make seats more favorable to their party in a slew of states, including multi-seat grabs in Florida and Texas. Democrats have had a much more difficult time, with only the California ballot proposition successfully withstanding legal challenges, while an effort to redistrict in Virginia and a push for potential 2028 redistricting in Maryland were both struck down by their state courts.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who has helped coordinate much of Democrats' redistricting efforts this year, applauded the court’s decision, calling it a “resounding victory.”

“The United States Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Virginia Supreme Court in May,” Jeffries wrote in a statement. “We are watching closely to determine if they apply the same standard here, or choose to do the bidding of the Republican Party again.”

This story was updated to include comments from Trump and Jeffries.

entries.title: Prosecutors Say Trayon White Is Trying to ‘Tamper’ With Jury Pool
entries.summary: The Ward 8 D.C. Council member, whose federal bribery trial starts this month, commented on jury selection in an Instagram video.
entries.content:
Federal prosecutors asked a judge on Thursday to “admonish” Ward 8 D.C. Council member Trayon White over a video he shared with his 87,000 followers on Instagram where he discussed jury selection for his upcoming trial on federal bribery charges.

“In the video, the Defendant makes a blatant attempt to tamper with the jury pool for his upcoming trial by appealing to race, making disparaging comments about the jury selection process, and inflammatory comments about a separate jury trial,” wrote U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro in a filing to U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras.

In the video posted Wednesday, White is seen standing in front of a D.C. court building, where he makes some of the first public comments on his trial — which starts Sept. 14 — while weighing in on the jury-selection process, which will begin the week before.

“I feel really good and encouraged about my trial. I’m in good spirits … I trust my legal team,” he said. “But I can’t do this without getting the opportunity to have a jury of my peers. I’m not going to say that all Black people support me, all non-Black do or don’t support me, I just want to make sure that those in my community in Washington, D.C., take this very seriously. It’s just about me, but it’s about us.”

White, a three-term lawmaker, stands accused of accepting tens of thousands of dollars from a D.C. businessman who wanted help landing more contracts with the city. The council member recently admitted that he accepted the payments, but has argued in court filings that he did nothing for the businessman in exchange. His defense attorneys have also said they may try to argue that he was entrapped by the government.

White is active on social media, but has also generated controversy with his freewheeling videos. In the video posted Wednesday, he said that only 22% of potential jurors in D.C. who are Black answer their jury summonses, and cited a murder trial that took place in Florida earlier this year where all Black jurors were dismissed by prosecutors.

“In America we have to ensure based on my Sixth Amendment right of a jury of my peers that I have a fair trial and a fair shake in fighting for my freedom,” he said.

“I’ve been elected two times … so I know there are people who do have faith in me and my work, but that’s not enough. I want to fight for my freedom and opportunity to have a fair trial. I’ve heard what Jeanine Pirro is saying about me, but we have to put the power in the jury of the people so I can get my side of the story out,” he added.

There have been past concerns that federal juries in D.C. don’t reflect the demographics of the city. During a criminal trial in 2023, defense attorneys shared data they said showed that 30% of potential jurors in federal trials were Black — compared to their 39% share of jury-eligible residents in the city.

But Pirro said White’s comments represented an “unabashed attempt to taint the jury,” and that they could prejudice the jury pool for the trial.

“For example, in one such comment, a person responds, ‘I agree. Everyone in this sweet city knows you were set up. We are targeted, especially when in an important position!!! Eyes wide open.’ In another comment, a person responds, ‘Praying that I get that summons. I would spend however long listening to case only to tell the rest of the jury NOT FKING GUILTY and that will not change,’” she said in the filing.

In a response filed Thursday afternoon, Warren Gary Kohlman, White’s defense attorney, said that in the video the council member “expressed nothing unlawful and, instead, expressly sought to uphold his constitutional right to a fair trial.”

“Moreover, the Government’s position threatens Mr. White’s First Amendment rights, in which he is entitled to express his opinion on his own case and on the workings of the federal criminal justice system in the District of Columbia,” wrote Kohlman. “As a practical matter, it is extremely unlikely at this point in time that Mr. White’s comments, expressly to encourage responses to jury summonses as required by law, could have an impact on the jury pool coming in next week for his trial, either for good or for ill.”

The issue of juries in D.C. has become a flash point over the last year, with some juries seeming to reject prosecutions stemming from the ramped-up federal presence and arrests in the city. One local group that has opposed federal intervention in D.C. has held educational events on how serving on a jury “is vital to safeguarding the rights of those who are most vulnerable to systemic biases.” Some critics have said that can amount to organized jury nullification.

The dustup between federal prosecutors and White represents the second time he has drawn attention ahead of the trial. Last month, Judge Contreras admonished White for a text message his council chief of staff, Sheila Bunn, sent to a potential witness for the prosecution. Bunn later told NOTUS the text message was sent in a personal capacity to a friend and that she had not discussed White’s upcoming trial with him.

entries.title: Jim Justice Is Considering Leaving the Senate to Run for Governor Again
entries.summary: The one-term West Virginia senator has had public tension with sitting Gov. Patrick Morrisey.
entries.content:
Sen. Jim Justice says he could run for his old job as governor of West Virginia in 2028 — while suggesting the state has experienced a “disappointing" slowdown since his successor took office last year.

Justice will “100%” consider a run against sitting Gov. Patrick Morrisey, he told West Virginia outlet MetroNews on Thursday. The two Republicans have had a number of public spats, and Justice contended the state has lost its “spark” since he left office in 2025.

“When I had the opportunity to be governor, we kept our foot on the gas, and we tried so, so hard to compete with other states,” he said. “We’ve gotta do that. We’ve got to continue to compete.”

Justice would have to exit his Senate office early to run, though he has not spent a long time in D.C. The senator reportedly commutes several times a week between D.C. and West Virginia via a private plane, and has stayed in hotels in the capital from “time to time” instead of finding permanent housing. Justice just recently passed his first bill since taking office in January 2025.

The relationship between the former governor and his successor has been tense since the gubernatorial election: Justice endorsed Morrisey’s opponent, Moore Capito, in the 2024 Republican primary, and Morrisey announced upon taking office that he had “inherited” a $400 million budget deficit from Justice’s administration.

On Thursday, Justice said the state has failed to invest aggressively in its coal and gas portfolio in recent years, which he said would be the state's best bet to support struggling families. He did not outright criticize Morrisey when asked to compare their leadership styles, however, and even wished the current governor well.

“As far as Patrick and everybody here, I hope they knock it out of the park and they knock it out of the park every single day, but we’ll make a decision and we’ll make a decision real soon,” Justice said.

Morrisey’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: House Democrat Says the Pentagon Sought NIH Funds for Defense Use
entries.summary: As the military faces a war-driven cash crunch, Rep. Rosa DeLauro said it would be “outrageous” to siphon that money from disease research.
entries.content:
The Pentagon, as it struggles with a budget crunch driven by the Iran war, sought access to billions of dollars Congress provided to another agency for biomedical research, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee said Thursday.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut said in a statement that the Defense Department had signed an interagency agreement that could give it access to funding appropriated to the National Institutes of Health, including money for the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. DeLauro did not say the NIH signed the agreement and described what transpired as a Pentagon “attempt.”

It also was not immediately clear how much money the Pentagon was seeking, where within the Defense Department it would go or what it would pay for. DeLauro’s office said NIH officials disclosed the effort after House Appropriations Committee Democrats pressed them for information.

“This secretive attempt to siphon research funds away from NIH is outrageous,” DeLauro said, calling for the agreement to be terminated. “It is no secret that the Department of Defense is facing enormous financial pressure because of President Trump's war of choice with Iran. But the Trump administration cannot make American patients, families, and scientists pay the price.”

The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases funding was appropriated for biomedical research aimed at developing treatments or cures for infectious diseases, including influenza, malaria, tuberculosis, HIV and Ebola, DeLauro said.

DeLauro accused the Pentagon of attempting to make up for shortfalls caused by the war. “These funds were provided for lifesaving medical research, not as extra money for the Department of Defense,” she said.

NIH confirmed that it had explored a partnership with the Defense Department but described the effort as a collaboration on medical technologies, which would enable faster responses to emergencies, rather than the funding question. NIH said it and the Defense Department had explored ways to collaborate on therapeutics, diagnostics and personal protective equipment to protect against infectious diseases.

“NIH enters into partnerships with numerous government agencies,” an NIH spokesperson said.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The push comes as the Pentagon searches for ways to cover a widening budget gap six months into the Iran war while it waits for Congress to approve its $95 billion supplemental spending request that mainly covers war costs.

The department says it needs the additional congressional funding to pay for combat operations, replenish munitions and sustain extended deployments. The Navy is facing a shortfall of between $6 billion and $8 billion as it contends with higher-than-expected war and personnel costs, its top admiral said last week.

The Pentagon has already taken steps to stretch its accounts. It has asked Congress for permission to shift $4.3 billion in previously appropriated funds, and the Navy has reportedly diverted money from payroll to cover combat costs.

This story has been updated with a comment from NIH.
entries.author: Joe Gould

entries.title: Trump’s 250-Foot Arch Will Soon Break Ground, Burgum Says
entries.summary: Excavation will begin at the Memorial Circle site over the next two weeks, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Thursday.
entries.content:
The first stage of construction on President Donald Trump’s 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C., will begin over the next two weeks, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Thursday.

“We are pleased to announce that after a very long wait (over 125 years!), we are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck,” Burgum wrote on X.

The new project follows a wave of construction and beautification efforts in the District as the president makes his mark on D.C.

The arch will be located at Memorial Circle, near Arlington National Cemetery. The scale of the project and its impact on the surrounding area have caused concern among some Washingtonians and lawmakers.

When questioned about the arch, Burgum often argues that many major cities across the world have these kinds of monuments — though Washington will have the “most spectacular and beautiful arch of them all!”

“Over 70 major cities/capitals around the world, from London, Paris and Rome to Madrid, Athens and New Delhi, all showcase beautiful arches,” Burgum wrote on Thursday. “Interestingly, Washington, DC, is the only major Western capital without an arch.”

Critics of the monument say it could obstruct D.C.’s skyline — adverse effects that the National Park Service addressed in the agency’s mandated review of the proposed structure.

The NPS wrote that a larger arch “would allow a less obstructed view through its central opening and provide new viewing opportunities,” and concluded that since the arch comes as the nation celebrates its 250th anniversary, any arch smaller than 250 feet would not be “representative of this milestone.”

A lawsuit challenging the arch’s construction is still pending in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. In April, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered the NPS to provide the court with at least 14 days’ notice prior to “commencement of construction, or demolition in preparation for construction.”

It was not immediately unclear whether Burgum’s Thursday announcement of excavation occurring over the next two weeks constitutes that notice.
